topic: Bulk and surface properties of matter including nanoparticles (chemistry only)
subject: chemistry

items.q: A particle is measured and found to have a diameter of 5 x 10⁻⁸ m. Which type of particle is it?
items.correct: A nanoparticle, 1 to 100 nm
items.misconception: A fine particle, PM2.5
items.why: The labels work against the sizes. PM2.5 carries a smaller number than PM10 and the word 'fine' is used in everyday speech for the smallest powders, so students rank the categories by the sound of the names rather than by the diameters printed next to them. Rank them by the numbers the specification gives: nanoparticles 1 to 100 nm, fine particles 100 to 2500 nm, coarse particles 2500 to 10 000 nm. The PM numbers are in micrometres, not nanometres, so PM2.5 already means 2500 nm - twenty-five times the largest nanoparticle.

items.q: Which list puts the three types of particle in order of increasing diameter?
items.correct: Nanoparticles, fine particles, coarse particles
items.misconception: Fine particles, nanoparticles, coarse particles
items.why: The labels work against the sizes. PM2.5 carries a smaller number than PM10 and the word 'fine' is used in everyday speech for the smallest powders, so students rank the categories by the sound of the names rather than by the diameters printed next to them. Rank them by the numbers the specification gives: nanoparticles 1 to 100 nm, fine particles 100 to 2500 nm, coarse particles 2500 to 10 000 nm. The PM numbers are in micrometres, not nanometres, so PM2.5 already means 2500 nm - twenty-five times the largest nanoparticle.

items.q: According to the specification, coarse particles (PM10) have diameters between which two values?
items.correct: 1 x 10⁻⁵ m and 2.5 x 10⁻⁶ m
items.misconception: 1 x 10⁻⁷ m and 2.5 x 10⁻⁶ m
items.why: The labels work against the sizes. PM2.5 carries a smaller number than PM10 and the word 'fine' is used in everyday speech for the smallest powders, so students rank the categories by the sound of the names rather than by the diameters printed next to them. Rank them by the numbers the specification gives: nanoparticles 1 to 100 nm, fine particles 100 to 2500 nm, coarse particles 2500 to 10 000 nm. The PM numbers are in micrometres, not nanometres, so PM2.5 already means 2500 nm - twenty-five times the largest nanoparticle.

items.q: An atom has a radius of about 0.1 nm. Approximately how many atoms wide is a nanoparticle of diameter 20 nm?
items.why: The figure quoted in 4.1.1 is a radius, but it is the only number students remember, so it gets used wherever a size is needed - including in 'how many atoms across' calculations, where a diameter is required. Read the quantity as well as the number. Radius 0.1 nm means diameter 0.2 nm, so a 20 nm nanoparticle is 20 divided by 0.2 = 100 atoms across, not 200. Using a radius as a diameter doubles every answer of this kind.

items.q: Nanoscience refers to structures 1 to 100 nm in size. This is of the order of how many atoms?
items.correct: A few hundred atoms
items.misconception: Several million atoms
items.why: The prefixes milli-, micro- and nano- are learned as a list of 'small' words without their powers of ten attached, and one millionth is the smallest number most students meet outside science, so it gets used for whatever sounds smallest. Fix the ladder: milli- is 10⁻³, micro- is 10⁻⁶, nano- is 10⁻⁹, each one a thousand times smaller than the one before. A 100 nm particle is 1 x 10⁻⁷ m, which is one ten-thousandth of a millimetre, not a tenth of one.

items.q: A cube of a solid has sides of length 2 cm. What is its surface area to volume ratio?
items.why: Students divide the larger number by the smaller, or take whichever order gives a tidier answer, instead of reading the order out of the name of the ratio. The name gives the order: surface area to volume means surface area first. Getting it upside down reverses the whole argument of this topic, because the inverted quantity gets smaller as particles shrink instead of larger.

items.q: The side of a cube is decreased by a factor of 10. What happens to its surface area to volume ratio?
items.correct: It increases by a factor of 10
items.misconception: It increases by a factor of 100
items.why: Students correctly remember that area scales as the square and then apply that scaling to the ratio, forgetting that the volume underneath has scaled by 1000 at the same time. Work with both: surface area falls by a factor of 100 and volume falls by a factor of 1000, so the ratio rises by 1000 divided by 100, which is 10. The formula 6 divided by x gives the same answer at once.
items.random_wrong: It gets smaller by a factor of 10

items.q: A 1 cm cube of a solid is cut into 1000 cubes each of side 1 mm. Which statement about the pieces is correct?
items.correct: The total surface area is 10 times greater and the volume is unchanged
items.misconception: The total surface area and the total volume are both 10 times greater
items.why: 'More pieces' is read as 'more material'. The 1000 small cubes look like far more stuff than the single block did, and nothing in the picture reminds students that the pieces came from inside the original. Check it: 1000 cubes of side 0.1 cm each have a volume of 0.001 cm³, giving 1 cm³ in total - exactly the original. Each has a surface area of 0.06 cm², giving 60 cm² against the original 6 cm². Volume conserved, surface area multiplied by 10.
items.random_wrong: The total volume is 10 times greater and the surface area is unchanged

items.q: A metal works as a catalyst. Why is it more effective as nanoparticles than as a fine powder of the same mass?
items.correct: The nanoparticles have a much higher surface area to volume ratio
items.misconception: Each nanoparticle has a larger surface area than one fine particle does
items.why: The phrase 'large surface area' is remembered from rates of reaction without the words 'to volume ratio' attached, and 'bigger surface area' sounds like a natural reason for a bigger effect. Say the whole phrase every time: surface area to volume ratio. A single nanoparticle is smaller than a coarse grain in every way. The advantage appears when you compare equal masses, because that mass is divided into vastly more particles and so exposes vastly more surface.
items.random_wrong: The nanoparticles are a chemically different substance from the metal

items.q: Compared with a material with normal particle sizes, what quantity of the same material as nanoparticles is likely to be needed to be effective?
items.correct: Less, because of the high surface area to volume ratio
items.misconception: More, because each particle has a very small surface area
items.why: The phrase 'large surface area' is remembered from rates of reaction without the words 'to volume ratio' attached, and 'bigger surface area' sounds like a natural reason for a bigger effect. Say the whole phrase every time: surface area to volume ratio. A single nanoparticle is smaller than a coarse grain in every way. The advantage appears when you compare equal masses, because that mass is divided into vastly more particles and so exposes vastly more surface.
items.random_wrong: More, because so many particles are needed to fill a space

items.q: A medicine is made using nanoparticles instead of particles of a normal size. What is the most likely advantage?
items.correct: A smaller quantity of the medicine is needed to be effective
items.misconception: A larger mass is needed because each single particle is smaller
items.why: The step from one particle to a quantity of material is skipped. It is true that one nanoparticle does very little, but students compare one nanoparticle with one bulk grain rather than comparing equal masses. Compare equal masses. One gram of nanoparticles has a far larger total surface area than one gram of coarse powder, and it is the surface that does the work, so one gram of nanoparticles goes much further. That is why smaller quantities can be effective.
items.random_wrong: The medicine is changed into a more reactive compound

items.q: A deodorant is made with nanoparticles rather than with fine particles of the same material. What is the main reason for this?
items.correct: A smaller quantity is effective, because of the high surface area to volume ratio
items.misconception: Each single nanoparticle has a much greater surface area than any fine particle does
items.why: The phrase 'large surface area' is remembered from rates of reaction without the words 'to volume ratio' attached, and 'bigger surface area' sounds like a natural reason for a bigger effect. Say the whole phrase every time: surface area to volume ratio. A single nanoparticle is smaller than a coarse grain in every way. The advantage appears when you compare equal masses, because that mass is divided into vastly more particles and so exposes vastly more surface.
items.random_wrong: The nanoparticles must be a new substance with different chemical bonds

items.q: A sun cream is made in two versions using the same metal oxide. With fine particles it blocks UV well but leaves a white layer, and 5 g is used per application. With nanoparticles it blocks UV equally well, is clear on the skin and 1 g is used, but how much passes through skin has not been fully tested. Which conclusion does this information best support?
items.correct: It works with less material and is clear, but its safety is not yet proven
items.misconception: It is better in every way, so the older cream should not be sold
items.why: 'Evaluate' is heard as 'praise' or 'describe the benefits', and the information supplied usually leads with the advantages, so students stop when they run out of positives. An evaluation that ignores one side scores badly however much detail it has. Take each piece of information given, sort it into advantage or disadvantage, and then say which outweighs which and why. A conclusion with no comparison behind it is not an evaluation either.
items.random_wrong: It must be safe, because it is already being sold as a sun cream

items.q: A factory can buy a catalyst as a fine powder, needing 50 kg at a cost of 2000 pounds, or as nanoparticles, needing 2 kg at a cost of 1600 pounds. The nanoparticle powder can become airborne, and its effects on the lungs have not been fully investigated. Which conclusion does this information best support?
items.correct: Less catalyst is needed and it costs less, but workers must be protected
items.misconception: The nanoparticles are certainly the safer option, as no harm is reported yet
items.why: Everyday experience says products are tested before sale, and students are not usually told the difference between 'no harm has been shown so far' and 'harm has been ruled out'. The technology is also newer than the time needed to see long-term effects. Being on sale shows that no unacceptable harm has been demonstrated yet, not that none exists. Nanoparticles are recent enough that long-term effects on the body and on the environment are still being researched, which is precisely why the specification asks students to explain that possible risks exist.
items.random_wrong: The powder is better, because nanoparticles always harm the workers

items.q: Which statement about the possible risks of using nanoparticles is correct?
items.correct: Their long-term effects on health and the environment are not fully known
items.misconception: There are no risks, because the same material is safe in its bulk form
items.why: Safety is treated as a property of a substance rather than of a substance in a particular form, and safety data at home and in the lab is always quoted per chemical, never per particle size. The whole point of this topic is that particle size changes behaviour. Nanoparticles are small enough to be breathed deep into the lungs or to pass into cells, and their huge surface area can make them far more chemically active, so bulk safety data does not carry over.
items.random_wrong: There are no risks, because the products containing them are on sale

items.q: A metal oxide is safe to handle as a bulk powder. Why does this not show that its nanoparticles are safe?
items.correct: Their very high surface area to volume ratio can change how they behave
items.misconception: The nanoparticles are made of different atoms from the bulk powder
items.why: Students are used to explaining a change of properties with a change of chemistry, because that is what almost every other topic asks for. A purely geometric explanation feels too weak to account for a large change in behaviour. Nothing chemical changes. Grinding a solid finer does not alter its formula or its bonding; it alters what fraction of its atoms lie on a surface. In a nanoparticle that fraction is enormous, and since reactions and interactions happen at surfaces, the same substance can behave very differently.
items.random_wrong: Each nanoparticle has a larger surface area than a grain of powder

items.q: Is a nanoparticle about the size of one atom?
items.correct: No. Nanoscience structures of 1 to 100 nm contain of the order of a few hundred atoms.
items.misconception: Nanotechnology works with single atoms, so a nanoparticle is basically one atom, or two or three at most.
items.why: 'Nano' is presented in the media as the smallest scale there is, and atoms are also described as the smallest things there are, so the two get merged. Students rarely have the atomic radius of 0.1 nm to hand when they meet the 1 to 100 nm range. An atom has a radius of about 0.1 nm, so it is about 0.2 nm across. Even the smallest nanoparticle, at 1 nm, is several atoms wide, and a 100 nm one is around 500 atoms wide. That is why the specification says nanoscience structures are of the order of a few hundred atoms, not one.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What happens to the surface area to volume ratio as a particle gets smaller?
items.correct: It increases. As the side of a cube decreases by a factor of 10, the surface area to volume ratio increases by a factor of 10.
items.misconception: A smaller particle has less surface area, so its surface area to volume ratio must be smaller too.
items.why: Both quantities do fall when the cube shrinks, so students reason about the top of the fraction alone and never compare the rates at which the two fall. Volume falls faster than surface area: surface area goes with x² but volume goes with x³. For a cube the ratio is 6x² divided by x³, which is 6 divided by x, so the smaller x is, the bigger the ratio. A 1 cm cube has a ratio of 6, a 1 mm cube has a ratio of 60.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What size are PM10 particles?
items.correct: PM10 particles are coarse particles with diameters between 1 x 10⁻⁵ m and 2.5 x 10⁻⁶ m, that is 2500 to 10 000 nm.
items.misconception: PM10 means the particles are 10 nm across, and PM2.5 means 2.5 nm across.
items.why: The nanometre is the only unit in use for most of this topic, so the numbers in the PM labels get read in nanometres. That places both categories inside the nanoparticle range and destroys the ordering. The PM numbers are diameters in micrometres: PM10 is 10 micrometres, or 1 x 10⁻⁵ m, and PM2.5 is 2.5 micrometres, or 2.5 x 10⁻⁶ m. Both are far larger than any nanoparticle; coarse PM10 particles are the ones often referred to as dust.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What is the surface area of a cube of side 2 cm?
items.correct: 24 cm². A cube has six square faces, each of area x², so the surface area is 6x².
items.misconception: The surface area of a cube of side x is x², so a 2 cm cube has a surface area of 4 cm².
items.why: The formula for the area of one square face is well known and gets used for the whole solid, especially when the working is done quickly and the drawing shows only the faces you can see. Count the faces: top, bottom and four sides, six in all. Surface area = 6x² = 6 x 4 = 24 cm², volume = x³ = 8 cm³, ratio = 3 to 1. Using x² instead of 6x² divides every ratio by six.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A use of nanoparticles carries a possible risk. Should it be rejected?
items.correct: Not automatically. The risk is weighed against the benefit, using the information given, before a judgement is made.
items.misconception: If there is any risk at all then nanoparticles should never be used for that job.
items.why: Risk is treated as a yes or no property rather than something to be compared with a benefit, and the language of 'risk' in the media is usually a reason to stop rather than a quantity to weigh. Evaluation means comparison. A small, uncertain risk may be acceptable where the benefit is large, and an equally small risk may not be worth taking where the benefit is trivial. State both sides and say which one your conclusion rests on.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Are nanoparticles too small to affect the body?
items.correct: No. Being small is what makes them a possible risk, because they can be breathed deep into the lungs and can pass into cells.
items.misconception: Nanoparticles are so tiny that they cannot possibly do any harm - there is hardly any material there.
items.why: Harm is associated with quantity, and a nanoparticle is imagined as an amount too small to matter. The idea that small size itself is the hazard runs against that intuition. Small size is exactly the hazard. Large dust grains are trapped in the nose and airways, but nanoparticles can reach the deepest parts of the lungs and cross into cells, and their huge surface area to volume ratio makes them chemically active where they arrive.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented
